Maltese is the national language of Malta, a Semitic language descended from medieval Andalusian Arabic brought to the islands during Arab rule in the ninth to eleventh centuries. It is the only Semitic language that is an official EU language and is written in the Latin alphabet rather than Arabic script, making it linguistically unique in Europe. The language has been extensively influenced by Sicilian Italian and more recently English through centuries of colonial and trade contact, with roughly 40 percent of its vocabulary deriving from Romance sources. About 400,000 native speakers live primarily on the islands of Malta and Gozo. The language faces pressure from English and Italian, and is considered vulnerable to language shift among youth, though transmission to diaspora communities remains a significant challenge due to the minimal speaker base outside the archipelago. A written standard was established after Malta's independence in 1964, and dialect variation exists between the islands and mainland communities. Maltese exemplifies how prolonged multilingual contact can create a language with a truly mixed heritage, drawing from both Semitic and Romance traditions. It shares core Semitic roots and morphological features with other Arabic languages despite its geographic isolation in the Mediterranean.
